title: Max Array Sum
directAnswer: Pick a subset with maximum sum where no two chosen elements are adjacent (you may skip freely). The recurrence is dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + a[i], a[i]): skip i, take i on top of the best up to i-2, or start fresh at i. This is the House Robber pattern generalised to allow skipping and negatives. O(n) time, and O(1) space once you keep only the last two dp values.

remember.formula:
dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + a[i], a[i])
prev2, prev1 = 0, a[0]
for i in 1..n-1:
    cur = max(prev1, prev2 + a[i], a[i])
    prev2, prev1 = prev1, cur
return prev1
rules: At each index you have exactly two choices: **take** it (then skip the neighbour) or **skip** it. That binary choice is the DP.
The third term `a[i]` (start fresh) matters because negatives in `dp[i-2]` can make taking the element *alone* better than adding it to a worse prefix.
Only the last **two** dp values feed the next one → collapse the array to two rolling variables for O(1) space.
Adjacent means index `i` and `i-1`; skipping more than one in a row is always allowed.
Initialise `prev2 = 0` so `dp[i-2] + a[i]` at `i = 1` correctly reduces to just `a[i]`.
whenToUse: Choose a subset maximising/minimising a value with a 'no two adjacent' constraint
Linear sequence where taking one item forbids its immediate neighbour
You can skip arbitrarily many elements (unlike fixed-window problems)
antiSignals: Adjacency wraps around a circle → House Robber II (run the linear DP twice)
Contiguous subarray required, not a subset → Kadane's algorithm
No adjacency constraint at all → just sum the positives
2D grid adjacency → grid DP, not this 1D recurrence
remember.takeaway: When taking an element forbids its neighbour, the answer at each position depends only on the answers two and one steps back. Recognise that and you've solved the whole House Robber family — including this skipping/negative variant — with two variables.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you model 'no two adjacent' as a take-or-skip recurrence depending on dp[i-1] and dp[i-2], and whether you handle negatives by allowing an element to stand alone.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Dropping the `a[i]` (start-fresh) term, so a negative prefix drags down an otherwise good single element; or using dp[i-1] instead of dp[i-2] when taking i (which permits adjacency).
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Name the House Robber pattern, derive the recurrence from the binary take/skip choice, then collapse the dp array to O(1) space with two rolling variables.

problemStatement:
Given an array of integers, find the **maximum sum of a subset** such that **no two chosen elements are adjacent** in the array.

You may skip as many elements as you like; the only restriction is that you cannot pick two elements that sit next to each other. Elements may be negative, so the optimal subset is not simply 'all the positives'.

Return the maximum achievable sum.
constraints: The chosen subset may be empty in some variants; here the recurrence allows a single element to stand alone
understanding: This is House Robber with a twist: you maximise a sum over a subset where adjacency is forbidden, but negatives mean 'take everything non-adjacent' is wrong. At each index you either take the element (and must have skipped its neighbour) or skip it — a two-way branch that yields a clean O(n) recurrence.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the array contain negative numbers?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — that's the whole point of the `a[i]` term. With only positives this reduces to plain House Robber.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does 'adjacent' mean adjacent in the array or adjacent in value?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Adjacent positions in the array — indices i and i-1. Values are irrelevant to adjacency.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the array circular (does the last element neighbour the first)?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No, it's linear. If it wrapped, you'd run the linear DP twice — that's House Robber II.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Must I pick at least one element?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The given recurrence lets a single element stand alone, so it naturally returns the best single value when all sums are poor. Confirm whether an empty subset (sum 0) is allowed.

examples.explanation: Take 7 and 6 (indices 1 and 3) → 13. Also 3+4+... gives less. 7 and 6 are non-adjacent and maximal.
Take 3 and 5 (indices 2 and 4) → 8. The negatives are skipped entirely.
Take 2, 5, 4 (indices 0, 2, 4) → 11, beating 1+8=9. Three non-adjacent picks win here.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Recurse Over Take / Skip
approaches.whenToMention: State it to expose the overlapping subproblems, then add memoization or tabulation to kill the exponential blowup.
hints: Stand at index i. You can either take a[i] — then the next allowed index is i+2 — or skip it and move to i+1. What's the best you can do from index i onward?
Write f(i) = max(a[i] + f(i+2), f(i+1)): take this element and jump two, or skip and step one.
This explores both branches at every index → 2ⁿ paths. Notice f(i) is recomputed many times for the same i — that's the cue for memoization.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each call spawns two recursive calls (take / skip), forming a binary tree of depth n → roughly 2ⁿ calls. Recursion depth is O(n) for the call stack.
approaches.explanation:
The most literal model: at every index decide independently to take or skip. If you take `a[i]`, you must jump to `i+2` because `i+1` is now forbidden. If you skip, you advance to `i+1` with no penalty. The answer from index `i` onward is the better of the two branches: `f(i) = max(a[i] + f(i+2), f(i+1))`.

**Why two branches and nothing else.** The adjacency rule constrains only *immediate* neighbours. Once you decide about index `i`, the rest of the problem is the *same shape* on a shorter suffix — a smaller instance of Max Array Sum. That self-similarity is what makes it a DP problem rather than a greedy one.

**Why greedy fails.** A tempting greedy is 'always take the larger of two neighbours'. It breaks on `[2, 1, 5, 8, 4]`: greedy might grab 8, blocking both 5 and 4, but the optimal `2 + 5 + 4 = 11` beats `1 + 8 = 9`. Local choices can't see the downstream cost, so you must compare full branches — hence recursion.

**Why we don't ship this.** The recursion tree has ~`2ⁿ` nodes, but there are only `n` distinct arguments to `f`. The same `f(i)` is recomputed exponentially often. For `n = 10⁵` this never finishes. The fix is to *remember* each `f(i)` — memoization (top-down) or tabulation (bottom-up).
approaches.insight: The exponential cost comes entirely from recomputing the same `f(i)` over and over. There are only n distinct subproblems, so caching each one collapses 2ⁿ work down to O(n). Spotting 'few distinct subproblems, recomputed often' is the universal trigger for dynamic programming.

dryRun.intro: f(i) = max(a[i] + f(i+2), f(i+1)). Out-of-range f returns 0.

java.explanation: Past the end there's nothing to add — base case contributes 0.
Take a[i], then jump to i+2 because i+1 is now forbidden.
Skip a[i] and move one step right with no constraint.
The best of the two branches — this comparison is why greedy can't replace it.

python.explanation: Out-of-range index returns 0 — the recursion's floor.
Pick a[i], skip the neighbour, recurse from i+2.
Leave a[i] out and continue from i+1.

pitfalls: Recursing to i+1 after taking a[i] — that permits adjacency and is wrong.
Forgetting the base case, causing infinite recursion or index errors.
Running it on large n — 2ⁿ never returns; you must memoize or tabulate.

approaches.name: Top-Down Memoization (Java) vs Bottom-Up Tabulation (Python)
approaches.whenToMention: Show you can express the same recurrence both ways — caching a recursion (Java) or filling a table (Python) — and that they're equivalent in cost.
hints: There are only n distinct values of f(i). Store each one the first time you compute it so the second request is a lookup, not a recomputation.
Top-down: keep the recursion but cache results in an array indexed by i. Bottom-up: drop recursion and fill dp[0], dp[1], ... in order using dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + a[i], a[i]).
Both visit each subproblem once → O(n) time and O(n) space. The only real difference is recursion-stack risk (top-down) versus an explicit loop (bottom-up).
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each of the n subproblems is solved exactly once and cached, so total work is O(n). The cache (memo array or dp table) holds n entries → O(n) space. Top-down also uses O(n) call-stack depth.
approaches.explanation:
Same recurrence, two equivalent implementations — and they're deliberately shown in different languages to highlight the trade-off.

**Java — top-down memoization.** Keep the natural recursion from the brute force, but back it with a `memo` array. Before computing `f(i)`, check whether it's already cached; after computing, store it. Each `f(i)` is now evaluated once, so the `2ⁿ` tree collapses to `n` real computations.

**Python — bottom-up tabulation.** Drop recursion entirely. Fill a `dp` array left to right: `dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + a[i], a[i])`. Because `dp[i-1]` and `dp[i-2]` are computed before `dp[i]`, every value is ready when needed. The answer is `dp[n-1]`.

**Why they're the same algorithm.** Both compute exactly the set of `n` subproblems once. Memoization computes them lazily, in the order the recursion happens to ask; tabulation computes them eagerly, in a fixed left-to-right order. Same time, same space, same answers.

**Where they differ — and why it matters here.** Top-down recursion uses the call stack: for `n = 10⁵`, deep recursion can blow the stack. In **Python this is acute** — the default recursion limit is ~1000, so a top-down solution would raise `RecursionError` on large inputs unless you raise the limit. That's exactly why Python is shown bottom-up: tabulation uses a plain loop and no stack depth. **Java** tolerates deeper recursion and the JIT handles it well, so top-down reads cleanly there. The lesson: when `n` is large, prefer tabulation (or an explicit stack) in stack-limited languages.
approaches.insight: Memoization and tabulation are two views of one DP: lazy versus eager evaluation of the same subproblem set. Reach for top-down when the recurrence is easier to *write* recursively, and bottom-up when recursion depth (especially in Python) would overflow the stack. Knowing both — and when each fails — is what separates a memorised solution from an understood one.

dryRun.intro: Bottom-up fill. prev terms shown; dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + a[i], a[i]).

java.explanation: null marks 'not computed yet'; a primitive int[] couldn't distinguish 0 from unset.
Cache hit — return immediately instead of recomputing the subtree.

java.line: int take = a[i] + f(a, i + 2, memo);
java.explanation: Take branch jumps two indices to respect adjacency.
Store before returning so each i is computed exactly once — turns 2ⁿ into n.

python.explanation: A single element has no neighbour — its own value is the answer; also guards dp[1] below.
Best over the first two: take one or the other, never both (they're adjacent).
Skip i, take i atop dp[i-2], or start fresh at i — the third term handles negative prefixes.
Last cell holds the best over the whole array. No recursion → no stack-depth risk for large n.

diagrams.title: Filling the dp table left to right
diagrams.caption: Each dp[i] reads only dp[i-1] and dp[i-2] — the hint that O(1) space is possible.

pitfalls: In Java, using int[] for the memo can't tell 'unset' from a real 0 — use Integer[] with null.
In Python, writing this top-down risks RecursionError at n = 10⁵ — tabulate or raise the recursion limit.
Forgetting dp[1] = max(a[0], a[1]); setting dp[1] = a[1] allows skipping a better a[0].

approaches.name: Rolling Variables — O(1) Space (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want once tabulation is on the board. Phrase it as 'dp[i] only needs the last two values, so two scalars replace the array'.
hints: Look at the recurrence: dp[i] depends only on dp[i-1] and dp[i-2]. Do you ever read anything older?
Replace the whole dp array with two variables — prev1 (dp[i-1]) and prev2 (dp[i-2]) — and slide them forward each step.
Initialise prev2 = 0 and prev1 = a[0]. Each step: cur = max(prev1, prev2 + a[i], a[i]); then prev2 = prev1, prev1 = cur.
approaches.complexityReasoning: A single pass over n elements with constant work per step → O(n) time. Only two scalars are retained regardless of n → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
The tabulation never reaches further back than two cells, so storing the entire `dp` array wastes memory. Keep just two rolling variables: `prev2 = dp[i-2]` and `prev1 = dp[i-1]`. Compute `cur = max(prev1, prev2 + a[i], a[i])`, then slide: `prev2` becomes `prev1`, `prev1` becomes `cur`.

**Why the three terms, restated for the scalar form.** `prev1` is the *skip* choice (carry the best up to `i-1`). `prev2 + a[i]` is the *take* choice (add `a[i]` to the best that excluded `i-1`). `a[i]` alone is the *fresh-start* choice — essential when `prev2` is negative, so a strong single element isn't dragged down by a bad prefix.

**Why `prev2` starts at 0.** At `i = 1`, the term `prev2 + a[1]` should mean 'take `a[1]` with nothing before it', i.e. just `a[1]`. Seeding `prev2 = 0` makes that fall out automatically, and it equals the `a[i]` term — harmless overlap.

**Why this is the version to ship.** Same `O(n)` time as tabulation but `O(1)` space, and no recursion stack to overflow — safe even at `n = 10⁵`. It's also the cleanest to state in an interview: two variables, one pass.

**Reconstructing the chosen subset.** If asked *which* elements were picked, the O(1) trick loses that information — you'd keep the full `dp` array (or a parent/decision array) and walk backwards. Mention this trade-off: O(1) space gives the value, not the witness.
approaches.insight: A recurrence whose window reaches back a fixed number of cells (here two) can always shed its array for that many scalars. This is the same compression that turns Fibonacci and Climbing Stairs from O(n) space into O(1) — recognise the bounded look-back and the optimisation is automatic.

dryRun.intro: prev2 = 0, prev1 = a[0] = 2. Slide two variables; cur = max(prev1, prev2 + a[i], a[i]).

java.explanation: dp[i-2] seed; 0 makes prev2 + a[1] reduce to a[1] at the first step.
dp[0] is just the first element — best over a one-element prefix.

java.line: int cur = Math.max(prev1, Math.max(prev2 + a[i], a[i]));
java.explanation: Skip (prev1), take (prev2 + a[i]), or start fresh (a[i]) — the full recurrence in one line.
Slide the window: old prev1 becomes the new prev2.
After the loop prev1 holds dp[n-1], the answer.

python.explanation: Three candidates: skip, take-on-prefix, take-alone. max picks the best.
Tuple assignment slides both variables forward in one step.
Final prev1 is the maximum non-adjacent subset sum.

diagrams.title: Two scalars sliding across the array
diagrams.caption: prev1 tracks the running best; prev2 lags one step behind it.

edgeCases.behavior: Loop never runs; prev1 = a[0] = 5 is returned. Single element is its own answer.
Every take term is negative; cur tracks the least-bad single element → returns -1. The a[i] term keeps it from compounding negatives.
i=1: max(1,2,2)=2; i=2: max(2, 1+3, 3)=4 → returns 4 (take 1 and 3). Adjacency between 2 and 3 correctly forbidden.

pitfalls: Dropping the a[i] term — negative prev2 then forces a worse sum than taking the element alone.
Using prev1 (dp[i-1]) instead of prev2 in the take branch — that allows adjacent picks.
Trying to recover the chosen indices from O(1) space — you need the full dp array for that.

commonMistakes: Omitting the start-fresh term a[i], so a negative prefix poisons an otherwise strong element.
Adding a[i] to dp[i-1] instead of dp[i-2] — permits two adjacent picks.
Writing the top-down version in Python and hitting RecursionError at large n.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Forgetting the start-fresh term
commonMistakesDetailed.why: On [-5, 10], taking 10 atop dp[i-2] = -5 gives 5, but 10 alone is better. Without the a[i] term you'd report 5 instead of 10.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Taking on dp[i-1] instead of dp[i-2]
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Adding a[i] to dp[i-1] lets index i pair with index i-1 — exactly the adjacency the problem forbids.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: int cur = Math.max(prev1, prev1 + a[i]);  // prev1 = dp[i-1]: adjacency allowed
commonMistakesDetailed.good: int cur = Math.max(prev1, Math.max(prev2 + a[i], a[i]));  // prev2 = dp[i-2]

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Top-down recursion in Python at scale
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Python's default recursion limit (~1000) overflows at n = 10⁵. Tabulation uses a loop and has no such limit.
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
for i in range(2, n):
    dp[i] = max(dp[i - 1], dp[i - 2] + a[i], a[i])

followupVariations.hint: Positives only — the same recurrence without needing the start-fresh term.

followupVariations.title: House Robber II
followupVariations.hint: Circular array — run the linear DP twice, once excluding the first house and once the last.

followupVariations.title: Delete and Earn
followupVariations.hint: Bucket values into counts, then it's House Robber on the value axis.

followupVariations.title: Maximum Subarray
followupVariations.hint: Contiguous (not subset) — Kadane's, the contrast case for the anti-signal.

patternNote: Canonical non-adjacent selection DP (House Robber family). Whenever choosing an element forbids its neighbour, the state two steps back plus one step back determines the answer — collapse to two scalars for O(1) space. Same shape as House Robber, Delete and Earn, and cooldown-stock problems.
